title: EPFL Demonstrates Millimeter-Wave-to-Optical Transducer with 67% Internal Efficiency - Quantum Computing Report
gist: EPFL demonstrated an integrated thin-film lithium niobate electro-optic transducer converting between 263 GHz millimeter waves and 1,561 nm telecom light, hitting ~60 kHz vacuum coupling and 67% internal conversion efficiency by matching optical and mm-wave mode volumes. Total off-chip efficiency remains tiny (1.6e-4) due to free-space antenna coupling; superconducting NbTiN resonators are the projected next step.

insights.claim: EPFL's Hybrid Photonics Laboratory built a thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) photonic molecule coupled to a sub-millimeter gold resonator that converts between 263 GHz millimeter waves and 192 THz (1,561 nm) telecom light with 67% internal conversion efficiency.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Raises the bar for quantum transduction, a key bottleneck for networking quantum processors over fiber.

insights.claim: The EPFL device achieved a vacuum electro-optic coupling rate g0/2π of 60 ± 8 kHz, exceeding microwave-domain electro-optic coupling rates by a factor of 60, with cooperativity up to 0.27.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Moving transduction to mm-wave frequencies looks like a route to much stronger coupling than microwave-band approaches.

insights.claim: Total off-chip wireless efficiency of the EPFL transducer is still only about 1.6 × 10^-4 because of poor free-space beam coupling into the integrated antenna.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Headline 67% is internal only; system-level efficiency is the gating metric before practical deployment.

insights.claim: The device resolved thermal background occupancy of 0.21 ± 0.08 photons, below the single-quantum limit, directly via optical sideband detection.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Shows the transducer can double as a sensitive mm-wave thermal photon detector.

insights.claim: Electro-optic vacuum coupling scales with frequency as g0 ∝ (ω/V)^1/2, but prior mm-wave transducers lost the benefit through mode-volume mismatch between sub-millimeter fields and millimeter-scale optical racetrack resonators.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Explains why geometric co-design, not just frequency, determines transducer performance.

insights.claim: EPFL resolved the mode-volume mismatch with two compact Fabry–Pérot microcavities (110 μm and 119 μm) defined by photonic-crystal mirrors in a suspended 400 nm TFLN membrane, paired with a ~165 μm quarter-wave gold resonator.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Compact TFLN cavity architectures are a fabrication capability to track among integrated-photonics suppliers.

insights.claim: Because the optical linewidth is about two orders of magnitude narrower than the mm-wave resonance, the transducer operates in a reversed dissipation regime where the thermal sideband serves as an uncalibrated internal standard for measuring cooperativity.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Self-calibrating measurement simplifies characterization of future transducers.

insights.claim: Coherent mm-wave-to-optical conversion could link cryogenic quantum processors and neutral-atom (Rydberg) registers over optical fiber without adding thermal load.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Transduction is an enabling component for distributed/modular quantum computing roadmaps across modalities.

insights.claim: Replacing the normal-metal gold resonator with a high-gap superconductor such as niobium titanium nitride (NbTiN) is projected to suppress ohmic damping and raise total transduction efficiency at liquid-helium temperatures.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Next-generation results hinge on superconducting materials integration; watch for follow-up demonstrations.
